Meanwhile databases struggle under heavy read traffic, so engineers place a cache in front of them; this layer stores frequently requested rows in memory. A good cache reduces latency, lowers load on disks, and lets applications serve many more users.

However fast a cache seems, it introduces a hard problem: keeping copies consistent with the source of truth. When a row changes, stale entries must be invalidated or refreshed; otherwise users see outdated values. Common strategies include write-through, write-behind, and time-based expiration, and each cache policy trades freshness against speed and complexity in different ways.

Along with its obvious gains, caching brings a thorny duty: tracking which rows sit in RAM, wiping out old data on a strict clock, and blocking a frantic flood of lookups that could swamp a primary disk array during busy hours; watchful tuning is vital.

Finally teams must measure hit rates, size each cache wisely, and watch evictions closely before calling the tuning work done.
